subtopic_detail: Rapid weight gain fourteen weeks into olanzapine treatment that has finally controlled a first episode psychosis
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 24 year old man in the early psychosis clinic. His first episode involved persecutory delusions and command hallucinations that persisted through an adequate trial of risperidone, stopped for intolerable akathisia, and then aripiprazole, stopped for lack of benefit.

He has been on olanzapine 15 mg at night for fourteen weeks and is now free of hallucinations, back at his apprenticeship and keen to stay on the medication that finally worked. His weight has risen from 74 to 83 kg over that period and his waist circumference is 104 cm. He eats takeaway most nights and has stopped playing football. He is not diabetic and has no family history of diabetes. His fasting glucose is 5.9 mmol/L, triglycerides 2.6 mmol/L and high density lipoprotein cholesterol 0.85 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 82 per minute, blood pressure 132/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Weight 83 kg, waist circumference 104 cm, fasting glucose 5.9 mmol/L (3.0-5.4), glycated haemoglobin 5.6 per cent (less than 6.0), triglycerides 2.6 mmol/L (less than 1.7), high density lipoprotein cholesterol 0.85 mmol/L (greater than 1.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of his metabolic changes?

options.text: Switch him to a different antipsychotic with a lower metabolic burden and taper the olanzapine
options.rationale: Switching is the first consideration when alternatives remain untried, but he has already failed both of the lower risk agents that would be candidates and has only just achieved remission. The relapse risk of another change outweighs the metabolic gain in this particular patient (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia).
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia

options.text: Halve the olanzapine dose so that the metabolic effect falls while some antipsychotic cover remains
options.rationale: Metabolic effects of this drug are only weakly dose related, whereas relapse risk climbs steeply below an effective dose in the first year after a first episode. Dose reduction is considered later in a sustained remission with specialist involvement (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia).
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia

options.text: Continue the olanzapine, add metformin and refer him to a structured diet and exercise program
options.rationale: Metformin added to an antipsychotic that cannot be changed produces a modest but real reduction in weight and improves insulin sensitivity, and it is the best supported pharmacological adjunct for this problem. Combining it with a structured lifestyle program gives a larger effect than either alone and preserves the treatment that achieved remission (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia).
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia

options.text: Give dietary advice at each review and repeat his metabolic screen again in twelve months time
options.rationale: Advice alone rarely reverses antipsychotic associated weight gain, and a twelve month interval is far longer than the recommended monitoring schedule in the first year of treatment. Screening intervals are measured in weeks to months early on (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia).
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia

options.text: Add topiramate as a weight loss agent and monitor his cognition and renal function during treatment
options.rationale: Topiramate has some evidence for antipsychotic associated weight gain but carries cognitive slowing and word finding difficulty that are particularly unwelcome in a young man returning to work. It sits behind metformin as an adjunct (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: People with schizophrenia die around fifteen to twenty years earlier than the general population, and most of that gap is cardiovascular rather than suicide, which makes metabolic care a core part of psychiatric treatment rather than an afterthought. Olanzapine and clozapine carry the greatest weight and glycaemic burden, and the largest weight gain occurs in the first three to six months of treatment. Monitoring includes weight and waist at every visit early on, with fasting glucose or glycated haemoglobin and lipids at baseline, three months and then at least annually. When the offending drug cannot be changed because it is the only agent that has worked, metformin plus a structured lifestyle intervention is the best supported response. Smoking cessation and blood pressure management complete the cardiovascular risk plan.
key_points: Weight gain on antipsychotics is fastest in the first three to six months of treatment
Olanzapine and clozapine carry the highest metabolic burden of the available agents
Metformin is the best supported adjunct when the antipsychotic cannot be changed
Structured lifestyle programs outperform generic advice and add to the drug effect
Metabolic screening occurs at baseline, three months and at least yearly thereafter
explanation.pearls: A weight gain of more than 5 per cent of body weight within the first three months of an antipsychotic predicts substantial longer term gain, which makes that threshold the practical trigger for adding metformin rather than waiting for obesity to become established.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia

subtopic_detail: Starting medication in a newly diagnosed adult who drives a heavy vehicle for a living
stem:
You are the psychiatrist seeing a 29 year old woman whose assessment, including collateral from her mother and school reports, has confirmed attention deficit hyperactivity disorder with childhood onset. She has never been treated.

She drives a rigid truck for a delivery company and has had two at fault low speed collisions in the past year, both while distracted. She smoked cannabis most weekends until two years ago and has not used it since. She has no chest pain, no exertional syncope and no palpitations, and there is no family history of sudden cardiac death or cardiomyopathy. Her mood is stable and she is not pregnant and uses an implant for contraception. Her physical examination including cardiovascular examination is normal and her thyroid function is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76 per minute, blood pressure 138/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Normal cardiovascular examination with no murmur, weight 68 kg, height 166 cm
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 1.6 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), full blood examination and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment plan?

options.text: Order an electrocardiogram and echocardiogram before any medication because of her occupational driving
options.rationale: Routine cardiac investigation before stimulant treatment is not required in an adult with no cardiac symptoms, no abnormal examination and no family history of sudden death. Occupational driving does not by itself create that indication (Source: Australian Evidence Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD).
source_refs: Australian Evidence Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Prescribe atomoxetine as first line because her history of cannabis use makes a stimulant unsuitable
options.rationale: Remote cannabis use with two years of abstinence is not an active substance use disorder and does not displace stimulants from first line, and treating the condition itself reduces later substance use. Atomoxetine is preferred when there is current stimulant misuse or diversion risk (Source: Australian Evidence Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD).
source_refs: Australian Evidence Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Offer structured psychological therapy alone and reserve any medication for a later review point
options.rationale: Psychological and skills based approaches are valuable adjuncts but have smaller effects on core inattention than medication in adults, and she has a safety critical occupational problem now. Therapy alone is a reasonable primary choice when a patient declines medication (Source: Australian Evidence Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD).
source_refs: Australian Evidence Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Record baseline pulse, blood pressure and weight, then start a long acting stimulant with review in four weeks
options.rationale: Long acting stimulants are first line for adult attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and require baseline cardiovascular observations and weight with regular repetition rather than routine cardiac imaging. Early review allows titration against symptom response and adverse effects before her next licence assessment (Source: Australian Evidence Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD).
source_refs: Australian Evidence Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Begin an immediate release dexamfetamine preparation dosed three times daily to allow flexible timing
options.rationale: Multiple daily immediate release doses give a fluctuating effect, worse adherence and greater diversion risk than a single long acting preparation. Short acting forms are used to supplement a long acting base or where cost prevents its use (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: The Australian guideline for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder recommends medication as first line for adults with moderate to severe impairment, with long acting stimulants preferred for adherence and smoother symptom coverage. Baseline assessment consists of cardiovascular history, family history of sudden cardiac death or cardiomyopathy, examination, and measurement of pulse, blood pressure and weight, with investigations reserved for those in whom this screen raises a concern. Stimulant prescribing in Australia additionally requires authority from the relevant state or territory health department, and the requirements differ between jurisdictions. Untreated disorder is itself associated with a higher crash risk, and treatment reduces it, so occupational driving supports rather than opposes effective treatment. Patients must be counselled that driving is not permitted while impaired and that licensing authorities have their own reporting standards.
key_points: Long acting stimulants are first line for adults with significant impairment
Baseline monitoring is pulse, blood pressure and weight, plus a cardiac symptom and family history screen
Routine electrocardiography and echocardiography are not required without cardiac red flags
Remote cannabis use with sustained abstinence does not preclude stimulant treatment
Stimulant prescribing requires a state or territory authority in addition to the clinical decision
explanation.pearls: Repeat pulse, blood pressure and weight at every dose change and then at least six monthly, because a sustained rise of more than about 10 mmHg systolic or 10 beats per minute is the trigger to reduce the dose or reconsider the agent.

sources.label: Australian Evidence Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

subtopic_detail: Dizziness and sensory disturbance four days after abruptly stopping a serotonin noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 34 year old woman who stopped taking venlafaxine 150 mg four days ago. She had been well for nine months after a single depressive episode and decided to stop when her repeat prescription ran out while she was away.

Since the second day she has felt light headed whenever she turns her head, has had brief sensations she describes as a zap through her scalp when she moves her eyes, and has felt nauseated and unusually irritable. Her sleep is broken by vivid dreams. She still enjoys her hobbies, has been at work every day, denies any low mood or loss of interest, and her appetite and concentration are unchanged. There are no thoughts of self harm. Her neurological examination is normal and her blood pressure shows no postural drop.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78 per minute, sitting blood pressure 118/74 mmHg with no postural drop, respiratory rate 14 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Normal cranial nerve, cerebellar and gait examination, no nystagmus, mood reactive with normal range of affect

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Diagnose an early relapse and increase her venlafaxine above the dose she was previously taking
options.rationale: Relapse presents with returning low mood, anhedonia and cognitive symptoms over weeks, not with dizziness and sensory zaps within days of cessation. Dose escalation would be right if depressive symptoms had genuinely returned (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Prescribe a short course of a benzodiazepine to cover the symptoms until they settle by themselves
options.rationale: Sedatives blunt the irritability and insomnia but do not address the underlying withdrawal and introduce dependence risk in a woman who needs a structured taper. Their use is confined to severe short lived distress where no other option exists (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Switch her to fluoxetine and then stop that agent after a fortnight without any further tapering
options.rationale: Substituting a long half life agent is a recognised strategy but is reserved for patients who cannot tolerate a gradual taper of the original drug. Using it first adds a second medicine and a switch related risk that a simple taper avoids (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Reassure her the symptoms will fade within a week and review her again if they have not resolved
options.rationale: Symptoms do usually resolve but she is significantly distressed now and untreated withdrawal is a common reason patients conclude they can never come off the drug. Watchful waiting suits mild symptoms in someone who is comfortable to continue (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Restart venlafaxine at her previous dose and reduce it gradually over several weeks with review
options.rationale: Reinstating the drug settles discontinuation symptoms within one to three days, which also confirms the diagnosis, and a gradual taper then allows her to stop successfully. Venlafaxine has a short half life and is one of the agents most likely to produce these symptoms on abrupt cessation (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Antidepressant discontinuation symptoms appear within a few days of stopping or markedly reducing a drug taken for more than about six weeks, and are commonest with short half life agents such as venlafaxine and paroxetine. The characteristic features are flu like malaise, insomnia with vivid dreams, nausea, imbalance, sensory disturbances including electric shock sensations, and hyperarousal with irritability. Separating this from relapse is the central clinical task, and the timing, the symptom profile and the absence of core depressive features do it reliably, with a response to reinstatement within days confirming it. Prevention is a slow taper, often over four weeks or considerably longer after long term treatment, with the final steps taken most slowly. Patients should be told about this phenomenon when the drug is first prescribed so that they do not stop abruptly when a prescription lapses.
key_points: Onset within days of cessation with sensory zaps and imbalance indicates discontinuation, not relapse
Short half life agents such as venlafaxine and paroxetine carry the greatest risk
Reinstatement produces relief within one to three days and confirms the diagnosis
Taper over weeks with the smallest reductions at the lowest doses
Relapse instead presents with returning mood and cognitive symptoms over weeks
explanation.pearls: Warn every patient starting a short half life antidepressant that missing more than a day or two can produce dizziness and electric shock sensations, because unrecognised withdrawal is a frequent reason people restart the drug believing their illness has returned.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

subtopic_detail: Sodium valproate maintenance in a woman of reproductive age who is not using reliable contraception
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar conducting an annual review of a 26 year old woman with bipolar affective disorder. She has had two manic episodes, the last three years ago, and has been well on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily since then.

She works full time, has a new partner of six months, and says she is not trying to conceive but is using condoms inconsistently and would continue a pregnancy if one occurred. She has never been counselled about the medication and pregnancy. Her mother took the same drug for epilepsy without problems, which she mentions as reassurance. Her mood is euthymic, she has no psychotic symptoms and her sleep is regular. Her weight is stable, her full blood examination and liver function are normal, and her serum valproate concentration is within the usual maintenance range.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic, no psychomotor change, no psychotic features, weight stable at 64 kg
data_table.Investigations: Full blood examination normal, liver function normal, serum valproate within the maintenance range, beta human chorionic gonadotropin negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Counsel her on the fetal risks, arrange reliable contraception and plan a switch to another mood stabiliser
options.rationale: Valproate carries a roughly 10 per cent risk of major congenital malformation and a substantially higher rate of neurodevelopmental impairment, so it should be avoided in people who could become pregnant unless no alternative works. Because she would continue an unplanned pregnancy, reliable contraception and a planned switch while she is euthymic are both required (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Continue the valproate unchanged and add high dose folic acid to reduce the risk to a future pregnancy
options.rationale: Folate supplementation does not prevent valproate associated neural tube defects or the neurodevelopmental effects, unlike its role in the general population. Recommending it as the sole measure gives false reassurance (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Continue the current dose and repeat her serum concentration and liver function every six months
options.rationale: Routine monitoring is appropriate for someone who must remain on the drug but does nothing about the reproductive risk that dominates this consultation. It would be the correct answer for a woman who cannot become pregnant (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Cease the valproate at today's visit and review her in the clinic in four weeks to assess her mood
options.rationale: Abrupt withdrawal of a mood stabiliser in bipolar disorder carries a high risk of rebound mania, particularly when stopped quickly rather than cross tapered. The change must be made while cover from an alternative agent is established (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Change her directly to lithium at a standard starting dose and defer discussion of pregnancy planning
options.rationale: Lithium is a reasonable alternative but it also carries fetal cardiac risk and demands its own preconception discussion, so deferring the conversation misses the point of the switch. Any change is made alongside contraception and planning, not instead of it (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Valproate is the most teratogenic of the commonly used mood stabilisers, with major malformations in around one in ten exposed pregnancies and impaired neurodevelopment in a substantially larger proportion, including a raised rate of autism spectrum disorder. Australian regulators require that it not be used in people who can become pregnant unless other treatments are ineffective or not tolerated, and then only with reliable contraception and documented counselling that is repeated at least annually. The window to act is when the patient is well, because switching during an acute episode is far riskier. Alternatives in bipolar disorder include lithium, lamotrigine and several second generation antipsychotics, each with its own reproductive profile that needs its own discussion. Where valproate genuinely cannot be replaced, the plan must include contraception the patient will actually use and a documented shared decision.
key_points: Valproate causes major malformations in roughly 10 per cent of exposed pregnancies
Neurodevelopmental impairment affects a larger proportion and is not prevented by folate
Counselling and reliable contraception are mandatory whenever the drug is used in someone who could conceive
Switch while the patient is euthymic, using a cross taper rather than abrupt cessation
Every alternative agent needs its own reproductive risk discussion
explanation.pearls: Document the pregnancy prevention discussion at least annually in anyone of reproductive potential taking valproate, since regulators treat repeated documented counselling, not a single conversation at initiation, as the standard of care.

subtopic_detail: Tachycardia with a rising troponin during the third week of a clozapine titration
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar on an inpatient unit reviewing a 27 year old man on day nineteen of a clozapine titration for treatment resistant schizophrenia. He is now on 250 mg daily and his psychotic symptoms have improved.

For three days he has felt tired and short of breath climbing the ward stairs, and the nurses have recorded a persistent tachycardia that has not settled with rest. He has a low grade fever and no cough, no sputum, no calf pain and no chest wall tenderness. His chest is clear on auscultation and his chest radiograph shows no consolidation. His white cell count and neutrophils are within the normal range. His C reactive protein has risen from 4 to 96 mg/L over eight days, his troponin I is 180 ng/L, and his eosinophil count is 0.9 x10^9/L. Echocardiography shows a left ventricular ejection fraction of 48 per cent.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 124 per minute, blood pressure 104/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 per minute, SpO2 96 per cent on room air, temperature 37.9 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 8.9 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), neutrophils 5.2 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), eosinophils 0.9 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5), C reactive protein 96 mg/L (less than 5), troponin I 180 ng/L (less than 16)
data_table.Imaging: Chest radiograph clear, echocardiography shows left ventricular ejection fraction 48 per cent with no pericardial effusion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Continue clozapine at the current dose and prescribe a beta blocker to control the tachycardia
options.rationale: Rate control masks the key monitoring sign while the myocardial injury continues, and continuing exposure to the drug is what drives the process. Beta blockade addresses benign persistent tachycardia only once myocarditis has been excluded (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Cease clozapine immediately and refer him for urgent cardiology assessment and monitoring
options.rationale: A rising C reactive protein with a troponin above twice the upper limit and impaired ventricular function in the fourth week of titration is clozapine induced myocarditis until proven otherwise, and cessation is the treatment. Continuing the drug risks progression to cardiogenic shock and death (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Halve the clozapine dose and repeat the troponin and C reactive protein in three days time
options.rationale: The reaction is not dose dependent in a way that makes reduction safe, and repeating tests three days later delays a decision that must be made today. Dose reduction is appropriate for sedation, hypersalivation or postural drop, not for myocardial injury (Source: RANZCP: Clozapine monitoring guidance).

options.text: Attribute the findings to the benign tachycardia of titration and continue the current monitoring schedule
options.rationale: Benign tachycardia is common early in titration but does not raise troponin, produce a rising C reactive protein or impair ventricular function. The near pair to separate here is a drug effect on heart rate from drug induced myocardial inflammation (Source: RANZCP: Clozapine monitoring guidance).

options.text: Start broad spectrum antibiotics for presumed pneumonia and review his response over the next 48 hours
options.rationale: He has no cough, no focal signs and a clear chest radiograph, and a normal white cell count with eosinophilia fits a drug hypersensitivity reaction rather than bacterial infection. Antibiotics would delay withdrawal of the causative agent (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Clozapine induced myocarditis occurs in roughly one to three per cent of patients in Australian cohorts, which is higher than international reports, and almost always presents between days 14 and 28 of titration. The early features are non specific, comprising fatigue, breathlessness, fever, flu like symptoms and tachycardia, so monitoring is biochemical rather than symptom based. Australian protocols check troponin and C reactive protein at baseline and weekly through the first four weeks, with a troponin above twice the upper limit of normal or a C reactive protein above 100 mg/L defining probable myocarditis and mandating cessation. Most patients recover fully after the drug is stopped, though a minority develop cardiomyopathy. Rechallenge has been performed in specialist centres with intensive monitoring but is not undertaken routinely.
key_points: Myocarditis clusters between days 14 and 28 of clozapine titration
Weekly troponin and C reactive protein monitoring through the first four weeks detects it before collapse
A troponin above twice the upper limit or a C reactive protein above 100 mg/L mandates cessation
Eosinophilia supports a hypersensitivity mechanism and often accompanies the reaction
Benign titration tachycardia does not raise troponin or impair ventricular function
explanation.pearls: Slower titration reduces the incidence, which is why Australian protocols increase clozapine in small increments over the first fortnight rather than following faster overseas schedules.
